meta.title: Dark pattern audit: product page and checkout
meta.applicability: QuickCart prices in ₹ and ships in India, so the CCPA Guidelines apply.
meta.note: Worked example from a test fixture. Screens normally also carry an 'image' path when a screenshot file exists.

summary.verdict: Checkout charges ₹159 of extras by default and reveals ₹52 of fees late. Three of these patterns have already drawn CCPA penalties.
summary.overview: 10 findings across 2 screens. The checkout cluster (pre-ticked add-ons, a shaming opt-out, an invisible decline) is the most urgent. Two product-page claims need data to confirm.
top_actions: Untick protection, donation and marketing consent by default (F1, F2, F5)
Replace “I’ll stay unprotected” with two equal buttons (F3, F4)
Show platform and handling fees on the product page (F6)

findings.title: Device protection plan pre-ticked at checkout
findings.limb: paid add-on added without consent (illustration a)
findings.evidence: The ₹149 device protection checkbox is checked when checkout loads. The ₹1,710 total includes it, although the user only added earbuds.
findings.why: A paid service the user didn't choose is added to the basket by default. This mirrors the Guidelines' own illustration of a pre-ticked paid ancillary service, and pre-ticked consent is barred by E-Commerce Rule 4(9).
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 2

score.rationale: Charges every buyer ₹149 by default at the payment step. Stacked with a shaming, low-contrast decline.

fix.summary: Present protection as an unselected offer with its price and cover. Add it only on an explicit tap, and update the total visibly.
fix.copy_after: Add device protection for ₹149? Covers accidental damage for 1 year. [Add protection] [Continue without]
acceptance_criteria: Fresh session: checkout total equals cart items plus disclosed fees, with no protection line
Protection is added only through a user click event, logged with a timestamp
Both choices use the same button component
fix.dev_notes: The checkbox renders with checked from server state. Default it to false in the checkout DTO.

findings.precedent: Zepto and PharmEasy (paid membership auto-added) were penalised; the Guidelines name auto-added travel insurance as an example.

findings.title: ₹10 donation pre-selected
findings.evidence: A ₹10 donation to QuickCart Foundation is checked by default and included in the total.
findings.why: The Guidelines list donations among items that can't be added at checkout without consent. The CCPA penalised an almost identical pre-selected ₹10 donation.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 2

score.rationale: Money taken from every buyer unless they notice and untick. Mirrors the PhysicsWallah order.

fix.summary: Keep the donation offer but unticked. Optionally show it after payment as a separate, clearly optional step.
fix.copy_after: ☐ Add a ₹10 donation to QuickCart Foundation
acceptance_criteria: Donation checkbox renders unchecked for all users
Total excludes the donation unless it is ticked in this session

findings.precedent: PhysicsWallah: pre-selected ₹10 donation, penalised by the CCPA.

findings.title: Opt-out says “I’ll stay unprotected”
findings.limb: fear wording on the decline option (illustration a)
findings.evidence: The only way to decline protection is a link reading “No thanks, I’ll stay unprotected”.
findings.why: The decline label uses fear to steer the user toward buying protection. This is nearly word-for-word the Guidelines’ “I will stay unsecured” example and IndiGo’s “No I will take risk”, which the CCPA required to be changed.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 3

score.rationale: Steers a purchase decision at payment, and mirrors the official illustration.

fix.summary: Replace with a neutral label that describes the action, not the user.
acceptance_criteria: Decline label contains no fear, loss or self-deprecating words
Copy reviewed against the confirm-shaming checklist before release

findings.precedent: IndiGo changed “No I will take risk” to neutral copy after CCPA intervention.

findings.title: Decline link is tiny and nearly invisible
findings.limb: decline obscured relative to accept (illustrations a, c)
findings.evidence: The decline link is 11px light grey text with a measured contrast of 1.92:1. The pay button is a full-width orange button.
findings.why: The design highlights the paid path and obscures the alternative. That is the core of interface interference, and the same contrast gap appeared in the McAfee renewal order.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 6

score.rationale: The visual asymmetry steers a paid choice at payment. The contrast was measured from the live DOM.

fix.summary: Make declining as visible as accepting: two equal buttons inside the offer card, both at least AA contrast.
acceptance_criteria: Decline text contrast is at least 4.5:1
Decline tap target is at least 44×44 px
Accept and decline sit in the same container with the same tap count

findings.precedent: McAfee: grey decline beside a red renew button.

findings.title: WhatsApp and SMS marketing consent pre-ticked
findings.evidence: “Send me offers on WhatsApp and SMS” is checked by default at checkout.
findings.why: Consent recorded through a pre-ticked box isn’t consent under E-Commerce Rule 4(9). The CCPA treated SpiceJet’s default promotional consent as a dark pattern. From May 2027 the DPDP Act also requires a clear affirmative action.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 4

score.rationale: Data and consent are taken by default from every buyer.

fix.summary: Untick by default, label it as optional, and record consent only on a user tick.
fix.copy_before: ☑ Send me offers on WhatsApp and SMS
fix.copy_after: ☐ Send me offers on WhatsApp and SMS (optional)
acceptance_criteria: Checkbox unchecked by default
Consent record stores the timestamp and source of the tick

findings.precedent: SpiceJet: default consent to promotional communications.

findings.title: “Inclusive of all taxes” price grows by ₹52 at checkout
findings.limb: limb (i): price elements not revealed upfront
findings.evidence: The product page shows ₹1,499 “Inclusive of all taxes”. Checkout adds a ₹19 platform fee, a ₹25 handling charge and ₹8 GST on fees, which first appear at checkout.
findings.why: Mandatory fees are revealed only late in the journey, after an all-in price claim. The CCPA penalised the same pattern at Zepto (handling fees at checkout) and FirstCry (GST added to “tax-inclusive” prices).
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 8

score.rationale: Every order pays fees not shown at the first price display.

fix.summary: Show mandatory fees with the first price, or fold them into the displayed price. Keep the same breakdown at checkout.
acceptance_criteria: For a standard order, product page price plus listed fees equals the payment amount
No mandatory fee line appears for the first time at checkout

findings.precedent: Zepto (handling charges at checkout); FirstCry (GST on tax-inclusive prices).

findings.title: Countdown restarts for every visitor
findings.evidence: “Deal ends in 00:15:00” ticks down, but a fresh browser session 5 seconds later showed the same starting value. The deadline is per-visit, not real.
findings.why: The timer implies a deadline that doesn’t exist, to push an immediate purchase. The CCPA penalised a recurring 24-hour countdown on a coaching platform as false urgency.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 1

score.rationale: Every visitor sees a fabricated deadline. Confirmed by a fresh-session reset check.

fix.summary: Use a real, server-side sale end that is the same for everyone, and end the offer when it expires. Or remove the timer.
fix.copy_after: Sale price valid until 30 Nov, 11:59 pm
acceptance_criteria: Timer end time comes from the server and is identical across two fresh sessions
After expiry, the sale price can no longer be purchased

findings.title: “Only 2 left” and “37 people viewing” claims
findings.limb: limbs (i) false popularity, (ii) understated stock (illustration a)
findings.evidence: Scarcity and popularity claims appear above the price. Both numbers stayed identical across sessions.
findings.why: If these numbers aren’t live, they are exactly the Guidelines’ illustration of false urgency (“only 2 rooms left, 30 others looking”). Unchanging values suggest hard-coded copy.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 1

score.rationale: Mirrors the official illustration. Stacked with the resetting timer on the same screen.

fix.summary: Drive stock from inventory with a timestamp. Drop the viewer count unless it’s real and time-boxed.
fix.copy_before: Only 2 left in stock! 37 people are viewing this right now
fix.copy_after: In stock: 2 units as of 2:10 pm
acceptance_criteria: Stock string is rendered from the inventory API response, never a constant
Viewer count removed, or sourced from analytics with a stated window

findings.verify: Ask engineering whether both strings come from the inventory and analytics APIs. Check the front-end bundle for the literal strings.

findings.title: App-install sheet offers only “Maybe later”
findings.limb: repeated request with no option to say no (illustrations a, c)
findings.evidence: A fixed bottom sheet pushes the app. The only alternative is “Maybe later” in 11px grey (contrast 1.61:1).
findings.why: Prompts with no real “no” are named in the nagging illustrations. Whether it returns on every page is unverified. The grey deferral also obscures the alternative.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 10

score.rationale: Annoyance and friction, not money. Mirrors the app-download illustration.

fix.summary: Offer a real “No” that is respected for 90 days, styled as a legible secondary button.
acceptance_criteria: After “No”, the sheet doesn’t reappear for 90 days on this device
Decline button contrast is at least 4.5:1

findings.verify: Navigate three pages in one session and revisit next day to confirm the re-prompt frequency.

findings.title: “Top pick” card may be an unlabelled paid placement
findings.evidence: A “Top pick: SoundMax Pro” card for a different product sits under the buy button with no Sponsored label.
findings.why: If SoundMax pays for this slot, it is an ad posing as an editorial recommendation. The Guidelines require ads to be identifiable, and put disclosure duties on sellers and advertisers.
provisions: Dark Patterns Guidelines 2023, s.4 + Annexure 1 item 9

score.rationale: Misleads without a direct charge. It is only an ad if the placement is paid.

fix.summary: If paid, add a visible “Sponsored” label at body size. If organic, rename it to explain why it’s shown.
acceptance_criteria: Every placement served by the ad system renders the Sponsored label component
Label meets AA contrast

findings.verify: Check the ad server or merchandising config for whether this slot is sold.

bait_and_switch.note: Listing, product page and cart show the same item and price.

trick_question.note: Consent wording is direct (the issue is the pre-tick, logged as F5).

rogue_malware.note: No scareware, fake alerts or suspicious redirects observed.

method.capture: Captured with capture_site.py (iPhone 13 emulation), including a fresh-session timer reset check, then scanned with scan_signals.py and reviewed against all 13 patterns.
limitations: Payment page and post-purchase emails not reviewed.
Stock and viewer counts can't be verified without backend data (F8).
sources: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
